doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Rock and roll, Elvis and country music
summary: He did not care for Elvis, but remembers Grandpa Jones on the Grand Ole Opry and later came to see country as a cousin to jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: How was the pop music scene at the time? You had rock & roll really making a big impact, you know, with Elvis and all those guys. Did that affect—

Yeah, I didn’t like Elvis. No. I says he’s a musician, I’m a musician, I says, his music doesn’t sound as good as mine. But he had that gyration going. Those knees going. So it’s show biz, you know, playing guitar. I didn’t care for country music. But strangely enough, as a kid I used to hear it every Saturday night on Grand Ole Opry. And there was one guy that I liked whose name was Grandpa Jones. The reason why I liked Grandpa Jones was because he used to talk about “that good old mountain dew.” And I loved the lyrics to that. And I used to just wait around and be a few minutes late for school just to hear that. Yeah. Grandpa Jones. But the rest of the country music I didn’t care for. But later on I discovered that it was like a cousin to jazz you know. And I also discovered that there were some very fine musicians involved in country music. And when I hear them in person I get more out of a kick watching them in person than I do listening. And then the lyrics are so simple and so down to earth and so basic that in a lot of cases they’re worth listening to.
